Only paths that start at A or G count, so the nodes linking A to G matter most: E and F share the top at 0.60, then C 0.50, with B and D 0.05 and the endpoints A and G 0." width="100%"} Percolation centrality (Piraveenan et al., 2013) measures the importance of nodes based on the proportion of 'percolated paths' that pass through them. Every node carries a percolation state between `0.0` and `1.0` (e.g., how infected, informed, or compromised it is), and shortest paths are weighted by the state of the node they start from. A node scores highly when it lies on many shortest paths leading *out of* highly percolated nodes, so it is the natural relay for whatever those nodes are spreading. This is particularly useful for: - finding the nodes best placed to pass on an infection or rumor from the nodes that already carry it - prioritizing interventions (vaccination, patching, monitoring) given the current state of an outbreak - re-ranking betweenness as a spreading process evolves, by recomputing with updated states When every node has the same state (the default is `1.0` for all), the score reduces to standard normalized betweenness centrality. Shortest paths are counted by number of hops, or by total edge weight when `weight=` is given, and on directed graphs follow edge direction. Like betweenness, the computation runs a shortest-path search from every node, so it can be slow on large graphs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [states]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, float] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Dictionary mapping nodes to percolation states, each between `0.0` and `1.0`. Keys are integer node IDs or string labels, and an unknown node raises a `ValueError`. Nodes missing from the dictionary get a state of `1.0`, so to mark only a few nodes as percolated you must give the others an explicit `0.0`. If `None` (default), every node has state `1.0` and the result equals normalized betweenness centrality. If the states sum to `1.0` or less (e.g., a single fully percolated node), every score is `0.0`. [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of an edge attribute holding non-negative weights, used as path lengths. Every edge must hold a numeric value (`"weight"` also accepts the edge weight of a weighted graph). If `None` (default), path lengths are counted in hops. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"percolation_centrality"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. Only used when `return_dict=` is `False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the scores as a dictionary keyed by node ID and leave the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), store the scores in the node DataFrame under `attr_name=` and return the graph for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to percolation centrality values. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, with the scores stored as a node attribute. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a key in `states=` does not match any node, a state lies outside `[0.0, 1.0]`, or an edge lacks a numeric `weight=` attribute or has a negative weight. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below is a five-node line A to E with a two-node branch (F, G) hanging off C. With the default states, every node is equally percolated and the scores are simply normalized betweenness: C, the junction, is highest. ::: {#b41e7c84 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("C", "F"), ("F", "G")]) ) scores = graph.percolation_centrality(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(n): round(v, 3) for n, v in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.333, 'C': 0.8, 'D': 0.333, 'E': 0.0, 'F': 0.333, 'G': 0.0} ``` ::: ::: Now suppose only A and G are infected. Paths that start at those two nodes are the only ones that count, so B and F (the first hops out of the infected nodes) climb from `0.33` to `0.6`, while D, which only carries traffic toward the uninfected end E, drops to `0.2`. Every other node must be given an explicit state of `0.0`: ::: {#4ed953b8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} states = {"A": 1.0, "G": 1.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0, "D": 0.0, "E": 0.0, "F": 0.0} scores = graph.percolation_centrality(states=states, return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(n): round(v, 3) for n, v in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.6, 'C': 0.8, 'D': 0.2, 'E': 0.0, 'F': 0.6, 'G': 0.0} ``` ::: ::: With `return_dict=False` (the default) the scores go into the node DataFrame, here under a custom column name: ::: {#aaaf7b21 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.percolation_centrality(states=states, attr_name="spread_risk") graph.get_node_df().select(["label", "spread_risk"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
